extracted.intended_audience: poets, writers, and readers interested in literary craft (early-18th-century aesthetic guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writers (poets, fictioneers, historians, essayists, and satirists) about how to affect the reader's imagination: how to use description, metaphor, allusion, personification, scale, and tone to delight or move a reader without falling into absurdity or cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mend and perfect Nature (poetic license)
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is the part of a Poet to humour the Imagination in its own Notions, by mending and perfecting Nature where he describes a Reality, and by adding greater Beauties than are put together in Nature, where he describes a Fiction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet may improve on or embellish Nature to satisfy the reader's higher ideas: combine admirable elements, intensify colours/scents, thicken woods, change vistas, alter winds and rivers, or invent new species. Use imaginative augmentation to please the Fancy, but exercise restraint (see 'Avoid Absurdities'). Examples in text: combining spring and autumn flowers together; making orange trees or myrrh in hedges; inventing richer flowers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to combine natural elements across time/space
rubrics_metrics.description: “He is not obliged to attend her in the slow Advances which she makes from one Season to another… He may draw into his Description all the Beauties of the Spring and Autumn, and make the whole Year contribute something to render it the more agreeable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive writers may compress chronology and mix elements from different seasons, climates, or ecologies for aesthetic effect (e.g., rose-trees and jessamines flowering together). This is a legitimate liberty of description to heighten delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid absurdity; preserve plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “provided he does not reform her too much, and run into Absurdities, by endeavouring to excel.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic liberties must stop short of absurd or impossible violations that break the reader's willing suspension of disbelief. Embellish nature, but avoid grotesque or inconsistent inventions that defeat pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairy/imaginary-writing requires a particular cast of fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is a kind of Writing… such are Fairies, Witches, Magicians, Demons, and departed Spirits… more difficult than any other that depends on the Poet's Fancy, because he has no Pattern to follow in it, and must work altogether out of his own Invention.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing about wholly imaginary beings demands an imagination naturally fertile and superstitious; success depends on the author’s unique imaginative temperament and invention rather than on real-world models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic, distinctive voice for non-human beings
rubrics_metrics.description: “their Sense ought to be a little discoloured, that it may seem particular, and proper to the Person and the Condition of the Speaker.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating speech for fairies/spirits/etc., avoid making them talk exactly like humans. Slightly ‘discolour’ their sense—give them particularity in thought and expression so they feel otherworldly and convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know legends, fables, and popular traditions for supernatural writing
rubrics_metrics.description: “he ought to be very well versed in Legends and Fables, antiquated Romances, and the Traditions of Nurses and old Women, that he may fall in with our natural Prejudices, and humour those Notions which we have imbibed in our Infancy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with folklore and traditional stories helps a writer hit the reader’s inherited beliefs and childhood associations—making fantastical representations more persuasive and pleasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personify abstractions plausibly (emblematical persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Author represents any Passion, Appetite, Virtue or Vice, under a visible Shape, and makes it a Person or an Actor in his Poem… We find a whole Creation of the like Shadowy Persons in Spencer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegorical personifications (e.g., Fame, Hunger, Sin) can be powerful when well-drawn; use vivid, consistent characterization so abstract qualities feel embodied and intelligible. The essay cites Ovid, Virgil, Spencer, Milton as exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical narrative: vivid scene-setting and measured unfolding
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is the most agreeable Talent of an Historian, to be able to draw up his Armies and fight his Battels in proper Expressions… We love to see the Subject unfolding itself by just Degrees, and breaking upon us insensibly, that so we may be kept in a pleasing Suspense.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historians (and narrative writers) should render events with lively particulars and pace their revelations so readers can form expectations and emotional investments; good scene-crafting makes the reader a spectator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scale and proportion to inspire astonishment
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nothing is more pleasant to the Fancy, than to enlarge it self by Degrees, in its Contemplation of the various Proportions… compare the Body of Man to the Bulk of the whole Earth… the whole Creation itself to the infinite Space…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ telescoping or microscopic comparisons (macro to micro) to evoke the sublime or the marvelous. Large-scale or minute-scale juxtapositions fill the imagination with grandeur or minuteness and provoke delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the limits of the imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let a Man try to conceive… and he will quickly find that he has no different Measures in his Mind… the Imagination… after a few faint Efforts, is immediately at a stand, and finds her self swallowed up in the Immensity of the Void that surrounds it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that readers can struggle with extremes of magnitude or minuteness; analogies that go beyond comprehension risk losing their affect. Use gradual steps and intelligible anchors when presenting enormous or tiny scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose apt, generally known allusions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Great Art of a Writer shews it self in the Choice of pleasing Allusions, which are generally to be taken from the great or beautiful Works of Art or Nature… it should be always borrowed from what is more known and common, than the Passages which are to be explained.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allusions are most effective when drawn from widely familiar, ‘great’ or ‘beautiful’ works or nature; they should clarify and ornament the passage rather than obscure it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor and likeness must be exact or agreeable
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Likeness ought to be very exact, or very agreeable, as we love to see a Picture where the Resemblance is just, or the Posture and Air graceful.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simile or metaphor should either be a precise, believable resemblance or an attractively graceful one; sloppy or strained likenesses offend the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid highly specialized, inaccessible comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: “great Scholars are apt to fetch their Comparisons and Allusions from the Sciences in which they are most conversant… I have read a Discourse upon Love, which none but a profound Chymist could understand.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not lean on obscure technical or scholarly references that will alienate general readers. Aim for illustrations accessible to the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination as essential embellishment of good sense
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is this Talent of affecting the Imagination, that gives an Embellishment to good Sense, and makes one Man's Compositions more agreeable than another's… it is the very Life and highest Perfection of Poetry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate imaginative imagery even in prose: it vitalizes sense and helps writing endure. Where imagination is lacking, writing may be dry despite other virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raillery/satire: keep kindness and conserve company
rubrics_metrics.description: “To make Raillery agreeable, a Man must either not know he is rallied, or think never the worse of himself… To rally well, it is absolutely necessary that Kindness must run thro' all you say, and you must ever preserve the Character of a Friend to support your Pretensions to be free with a Man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical or teasing writing should be tempered with evident goodwill; it should not expose or humiliate but should preserve amicable relation and social harmony. Effective raillery leaves the target uninjured or complicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid malicious ridicule (do not take pleasure in others' pain)
rubrics_metrics.description: “_Acetus_ has no regard to the Modesty or Weakness of the Person he rallies… He has no Mercy in making the Onset… It is, methinks, below the Character of Men of Humanity and Good-manners, to be capable of Mirth while there is any one of the Company in Pain and Disorder.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from cruelty or schadenfreude in humorous or satirical writing; attacks that produce genuine hurt are condemned and socially corrosive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soften satire by shared fault or self-deprecation
rubrics_metrics.description: “_Minutius_ has a Wit that conciliates a Man's Love… by insinuating that he himself is guilty of the same Imperfection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make raillery palatable by implying the speaker shares the foible, or by self-mockery—this keeps the target in good countenance and fosters camaraderie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct satire at vice, not at persons
rubrics_metrics.description: “the most agreeable Kind of it; and that to me appears when the Satyr is directed against Vice, with an Air of Contempt of the Fault, but no Ill-will to the Criminal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim moral satire at faults and vices rather than humiliating individuals; preserve charity toward the person even while condemning the behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the reader feel better (agreeable writerly aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The good Writer makes his Reader better pleased with himself, and the agreeable Man makes his Friends enjoy themselves, rather than him, while he is in their Company.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key aim of agreeable writing is to enhance the reader's pleasure and self-regard; style and tone should favor the reader's enjoyment and communal feeling over ostentatious display of the author's wit.
